lessons.title: What is Social Media Management and How to Get Started?
objectives: Describe what a social media manager is actually paid to do
Separate the work from the hobby of being good at social media
Decide which platforms a given business should be on
lessons.notes:
A social media manager runs a business's accounts so the owner does not have to. That is a job, and it is different from being personally good at posting.

WHAT THE JOB CONTAINS: deciding what to post and when, making or commissioning the content, scheduling it, replying to comments and messages, watching what works, and reporting on it. Modules 3 and 4 cover the calendar and the reporting in detail; this lesson is the shape of the whole thing.

WHAT IT IS NOT. It is not posting when inspired. It is not chasing follower counts. And it is not guaranteeing sales — you control what goes out and how the audience is handled, not whether the product is any good or priced correctly. Be clear about that boundary before you take money, because a client who believes you promised sales will be disappointed on a schedule.

CHOOSING PLATFORMS FOR A CLIENT — the question is where their customers already are, not where you enjoy spending time. For most small businesses here that means starting with a small number and doing them properly. A shop that posts well on two platforms beats one that posts weakly on five, and spreading thin is the commonest mistake in beginner account management.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — the channels that matter in this market are not always the ones in international courses. WHATSAPP is where a great deal of local selling actually happens: Status posts reach existing customers who already saved the number, and Business features like a catalogue and quick replies do real work. For many shops, WhatsApp plus one public platform outperforms an elaborate presence elsewhere. FACEBOOK remains heavily used across a wide age range here and is often where the buying audience is, even when it feels less fashionable. TIKTOK and INSTAGRAM reach younger audiences and reward video. If you manage accounts for local businesses and ignore WhatsApp because no tutorial mentioned it, you are leaving out the channel their customers actually use.
lessons.practice: Pick three local businesses you know and, for each, write where their customers most plausibly are and which two channels you would run. Then look at what those businesses are actually doing now. Where your answer differs from their behaviour, write one sentence on why — that reasoning is what you will be selling.

quiz.question: What should decide which platforms a client is on?
options: Where their customers already are, not where the manager prefers to work
Being present on as many as possible

quiz.question: Which boundary should be set before taking a client's money?
options: That you control the posting and the audience handling, not whether the product sells
That you cannot be contacted at weekends
That the client must supply all photographs
That results take at least a year

lessons.title: Master Social Media Like a Pro
objectives: Write a post that earns attention in the first line
Match the format to the platform instead of cross-posting identically
Build the habit of consistency over occasional brilliance
lessons.notes:
The craft of the individual post, which is the part you will repeat thousands of times.

THE FIRST LINE IS THE WHOLE BATTLE. People are scrolling, and they decide in a fraction of a second. Open with the thing that matters — the offer, the surprising fact, the question they actually have. Never open with 'We are excited to announce'. Nobody has ever stopped scrolling for that sentence.

ONE POST, ONE IDEA. A post that says three things says none. If there are three things, that is three posts, which is a problem solved rather than a problem.

SAY WHAT TO DO NEXT. Come to the shop, send a message, save this, check the price list. A post with no next step is a post that cannot be judged as working or not.

FORMAT FOLLOWS PLATFORM. The same message needs different clothes: short and visual on Instagram, conversational on Facebook, vertical video with sound-off subtitles on TikTok, a quick image on WhatsApp Status. Copying one post identically to four platforms is visible to everyone and reads as nobody being in charge.

CONSISTENCY BEATS BRILLIANCE. Three ordinary posts a week for six months does more than one excellent post a month. This is the single most reliable finding in the whole field and the hardest to act on, which is exactly why businesses pay someone else to do it.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — write for the conditions people are actually in. Most of your audience is on a phone, on a data bundle, often with autoplay off, frequently in a noisy place. So: put the message in the first line where it survives being truncated; caption every video, because it will be watched without sound; keep images light enough to load on a weak connection; and write in plain language, mixing English and Kiswahili where that is how the audience speaks. A post that requires a good connection to understand has already lost most of the people it was for.
lessons.practice: Take one message a real business needs to communicate and write it four ways — Instagram, Facebook, a TikTok script, and a WhatsApp Status. Change the format, not just the length. Then rewrite every first line until you would stop scrolling for it yourself, and check each one still makes sense if the reader sees only that line.

quiz.question: What decides whether a post is read?
options: The first line, since people decide in a fraction of a second while scrolling
The quality of the image alone

quiz.question: Why caption every video?
options: Much of the audience watches without sound

lessons.title: Hootsuite Platform Training Course
objectives: Schedule content in advance instead of posting live every day
Use one place to see everything that is going out
Know what scheduling tools cannot do for you
lessons.notes:
A scheduling tool lets you write a week of posts in one sitting and have them publish themselves. Hootsuite is one of several; the thinking transfers to any of them, and Module 3 already covers the calendar that feeds it.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS: batching is what makes this work profitable. Posting live every day means being interrupted every day, and you cannot run five clients that way. One focused session per client per week, scheduled out, is the difference between a job and a treadmill.

WHAT THESE TOOLS GIVE YOU: one calendar view of everything going out, several accounts in one place, posts queued in advance, and usually a single stream of incoming comments and messages so nothing is missed.

WHAT THEY CANNOT DO. They do not write the content, they do not reply for you, and they do not know when something has gone wrong. A scheduled campaign running through a national tragedy, an accident involving the client, or a day of protest looks careless at best. Check your queue against the news before it publishes, and know how to pause everything in one click.

SCHEDULING DOES NOT MEAN ABSENCE. The account still needs a person in it — replying, watching, adjusting. A perfectly scheduled account with unanswered comments is worse than an irregular one that talks back.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — two practical constraints. Paid tools are priced in foreign currency and are a real monthly cost against local fees, so start with the free scheduling built into the platforms themselves, which handles most of what a small business needs, and move to a paid tool only when the number of accounts justifies it. And not everything can be scheduled by a third-party tool — WhatsApp Status in particular is a manual, daily job. Build that into your working routine and your price rather than discovering it in week two.
lessons.practice: Take one client or imagined business and schedule a full week of posts in a single sitting, using the free scheduling in the platforms themselves. Time the session. Then write your own pre-publish check: what you look at before a queue goes out, and how you would pause everything if something happened.

quiz.question: Why does batching and scheduling matter commercially?
options: It lets one person run several accounts, since posting live means being interrupted daily
It is cheaper than posting manually

quiz.question: What must you do before a scheduled queue publishes?
options: Check it against the news, and know how to pause everything quickly

lessons.title: Free Social Media Training with Hootsuite Academy
objectives: Use free industry training to build credibility you do not yet have
Judge which certifications are worth the time
Turn learning into something a client can see
lessons.notes:
Free training from the platforms and the major tools is genuinely useful when you have no client history, for one specific reason: it gives you something verifiable to point at while your portfolio is still small.

WHAT IS WORTH DOING, roughly in order: the training published by the platforms themselves, because it is authoritative and free; the free courses from the big scheduling tools; and analytics training, because reading numbers is the part most beginners cannot do and clients most want explained.

HOW TO JUDGE ONE. Does it teach something you will use next week? Is it free or genuinely cheap? Is the issuer recognisable to a client? A certificate from an organisation nobody has heard of persuades nobody, and there is a whole industry selling those.

BE HONEST ABOUT WHAT IT PROVES. A certificate proves you sat through a course. It does not prove you can run an account, and no experienced client believes otherwise. Use it as supporting evidence next to actual work, never in place of it.

MAKE THE LEARNING VISIBLE. The useful move is not the badge; it is doing the thing. Take what you learned, apply it to a real account — your own, or a business you help — and write up what changed. 'I restructured this account's posting and replies, and here is what happened over six weeks' is worth more than any certificate, and it is a portfolio piece as well as proof.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — three cautions for spending time and money here. Courses that promise clients or income rather than skills are selling hope; be sceptical. Anything requiring a significant payment before you have earned anything is a bad trade when free training from the platforms themselves exists. And these courses are video-heavy, so download over wifi where you can rather than working through them on a bundle. Learn the durable thing — audience, message, consistency, measurement — because platform features change every year and the training chases them.
lessons.practice: Complete one free course from a platform or major tool this week, then immediately apply one specific thing it taught to a real account and note what changed after two weeks. Write that up in a short paragraph: what you changed, why, and what happened. That paragraph is worth more to a client than the certificate.

quiz.question: What does a certificate actually prove?
options: That you completed a course - not that you can run an account
That you are qualified to charge a professional rate
That your work meets an industry standard

quiz.question: What is the most valuable thing to do with free training?
options: Apply one thing to a real account and write up what changed
Collect as many certificates as possible
List every course on your profile

lessons.title: How to Create Content Pillars for Social Media
objectives: Define a small set of themes that every post belongs to
Stop the daily question of what to post today
Balance selling against the content that earns the right to sell
lessons.notes:
Content pillars are three to five themes a business posts about, and every post belongs to one. Module 3 gave you the calendar; pillars are what fills it without the blank-page panic.

WHY THEY WORK. Without them, every day starts with 'what shall we post', which is exhausting and produces drift. With them, the question becomes 'which pillar is due', which is answerable in seconds. This is the single change that makes managing several accounts possible.

A SET THAT WORKS for most small businesses:
- THE PRODUCT. What is for sale, what is new, what is in stock, prices.
- PROOF. Customers using it, testimonials, before and after, work delivered.
- USEFUL. Something the audience benefits from whether or not they buy — how to choose, how to care for it, a common mistake.
- HUMAN. Who is behind the business. The owner, the workshop, the morning setup. This consistently outperforms polished material, and small businesses under-use it because it feels unprofessional. It is not.

THE BALANCE. Most accounts sell too hard, and the audience quietly stops looking. Most of what you post should be useful, proof or human, with selling a smaller share — though when you do sell, sell clearly, with the price and the next step. Soft, vague selling is the worst of both.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — pillars make delegation and pricing possible, which is the commercial point. Once a business has four pillars, you can brief a photographer, tell the owner what to send you, and produce a month in one session. It also gives you the sentence that wins the client: 'Here are the four things your account will talk about, and here is roughly how often.' That is a plan. The competition is offering posts.

One local note: a pillar built on a fixed weekly rhythm works well where people check in regularly — a price list every Monday, a customer story every Friday — because audiences here are often on the account daily through Status and Stories rather than weekly.
lessons.practice: Choose one business and define four pillars, each with a one-line description and three example post ideas — twelve ideas in total. Then plan a two-week calendar drawing from them in rotation, and check the balance: count how many posts are selling versus useful, proof or human. Adjust until selling is the smaller share.

quiz.question: What problem do content pillars solve?
options: The daily blank-page question of what to post, replaced by which pillar is due

quiz.question: Which pillar do small businesses most often under-use?
options: Human - the owner, the workshop, the people behind the business

lessons.title: How to Find Your Target Audience on Social Media
objectives: Describe an audience specifically enough to write for one person
Find out what an audience actually wants rather than guessing
Use audience knowledge to change what gets posted
lessons.notes:
'Everyone' is not an audience, and content written for everyone reads as written for nobody. The work is to get specific enough that you can picture one person and write to them.

WHAT SPECIFIC LOOKS LIKE. Not 'women aged 18 to 45'. Rather: a woman running a small salon in a busy estate, who buys supplies monthly, checks her phone between clients, decides on price and reliability, and asks her WhatsApp groups before trying somewhere new. Now you know what to post, when, and what objection to answer.

WHERE THE INFORMATION ACTUALLY IS, and it is not a demographics dashboard:
- THE CLIENT'S OWN CUSTOMERS. Ask the owner who actually buys. They know, and nobody asks them.
- THE MESSAGES AND COMMENTS. Every question asked repeatedly is a post waiting to be written. 'Do you deliver?' asked eleven times is not an inconvenience, it is content.
- COMPETITORS' ACCOUNTS. Read the comments under their posts, which is where people say what they actually want and what annoyed them.
- THE PLATFORM'S OWN AUDIENCE DATA, once there is enough of it, which tells you when people are actually online rather than when you assume.

THEN CHANGE SOMETHING. Audience research that does not alter the posting was a waste of an afternoon. It should change what you post about, when you post, the language you use, and which objection every caption answers.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — two things specific to here. LANGUAGE is a real decision: English, Kiswahili, Sheng, or a mix, and it should follow how the audience actually speaks rather than what feels formal. Getting this wrong makes a business sound like an outsider to its own customers. And WHEN people are online follows the day people actually have — early morning before work, the commute, lunch, and the evening after they are home. Check the account's own data rather than trusting posting-time advice written for another country.
lessons.practice: Write one audience description of at least six sentences for a real business, specific enough to picture one person. Then collect evidence: ask the owner who buys, read fifty comments or messages on their account or a competitor's, and list every question asked more than once. Turn the top five questions into five posts.

quiz.question: Where is the most useful audience information?
options: The client's own customers, and the questions repeatedly asked in comments and messages

quiz.question: A question is asked eleven times in the messages. What is it?
options: A post waiting to be written
A sign the audience is wrong
